Gaṅgāpeyyālavagga Pācīnādisutta (The Discourse on the East, etc. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of water extending an hundred yojanas toward the east, a hundred yojanas toward the west, a hundred yojanas toward the north, and a hundred yojanas toward the south. A man would come along carrying a bowl or a cup and think: ‘I will drain this great mass of water with my bowl or cup, and I will dry it up and bring it to its end. Bhikkhus, what do you think? Would that man be able to drain that great mass of water with his bowl or cup, and to dry it up and bring it to its end? “It would not be easy for him to do so, Bhante. “Because of what reason? “Because that great mass of water is vast, Bhante, and the man’s effort is small. “So too, bhikkhus, when one has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power, made them a vehicle, made them a basis, established them, and maintained them, one can—by realizing it for oneself with direct knowledge—wield the various kinds of psychic potency: being one, one becomes many; having become many, one becomes one; one appears and vanishes; one goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as if through space; one dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; one walks on water without sinking as if it were earth; seated cross-legged, one travels in space like a bird; with one hand one touches and strokes the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; one exercises mastery with the body as far as the brahmā world. This, bhikkhus, is the first fruit of recluseship, visible here and now, more excellent than the previous state, more sublime than the previous state, which those who have entered the path have rightly realized. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of water extending an hundred yojanas toward the east... [as above] ...a hundred yojanas toward the south. A man would come along carrying a bowl or a cup and think: ‘I will scoop up some of this great mass of water with my bowl or cup, take it across the great ocean, and pour it out on the other shore. Bhikkhus, what do you think? Would that man be able to scoop up some of this great mass of water with his bowl or cup, take it across the great ocean, and pour it out on the other shore? “It would not be easy for him to do so, Bhante. “Because of what reason? “Because that great mass of water is vast, Bhante, and the man’s effort is small. “So too, bhikkhus, when one has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power... [as above] ...one can—by realizing it for oneself with direct knowledge—wield the various kinds of psychic potency... [as above] ...one exercises mastery with the body as far as the brahmā world. This, bhikkhus, is the second fruit of recluseship, visible here and now, more excellent than the previous state, more sublime than the previous state, which those who have entered the path have rightly realized. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of water extending an hundred yojanas toward the east... [as above] ...a hundred yojanas toward the south. A man would come along carrying a boat made of leather or a skin-bag and think: ‘I will cross over from this shore to the further shore of this great mass of water. Bhikkhus, what do you think? Would that man be able to cross over from this shore to the further shore of this great mass of water? “He would be able to do so, Bhante. “Because of what reason? “Because that great mass of water is vast, Bhante, and the man’s means are great. “So too, bhikkhus, when one has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power... [as above] ...one can—by realizing it for oneself with direct knowledge—wield the various kinds of psychic potency... [as above] ...one exercises mastery with the body as far as the brahmā world. This, bhikkhus, is the third fruit of recluseship, visible here and now, more excellent than the previous state, more sublime than the previous state, which those who have entered the path have rightly realized.

“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of water extending an hundred yojanas toward the east... [as above] ...a hundred yojanas toward the south. A man would come along carrying a raft made of grass, reeds, and branches and think: ‘I will cross over from this shore to the further shore of this great mass of water by means of this raft. Bhikkhus, what do you think? Would that man be able to cross over from this shore to the further shore of this great mass of water? “He would be able to do so, Bhante. “Because of what reason? “Because that great mass of water is vast, Bhante, and the man’s means are great. “So too, bhikkhus, when one has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power... The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four right endeavors.
Which four?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.

One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
These, monks, are the four right endeavors.

“Just as, monks, the river Ganges slants, slopes, and inclines toward the east, even so, monks, a monk who develops and cultivates the four right strivings slants, slopes, and inclines toward Nibbāna.
And how, monks, does a monk who develops and cultivates the four right strivings slant, slope, and incline toward Nibbāna? [The Buddha then explained each of the four right strivings.]”
In this case, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

“He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk who develops and cultivates the four right endeavors inclines toward Nibbāna, slants toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna.
The twelfth.
The first section, the Gaṅgāpeyyāla.
(The Gaṅgāpeyyāla of the Saṃyutta on the Right Strivings is to be expanded by way of the right strivings.
Its summary verse:
Six flow toward the east,
and six flow toward the ocean;
these two sets of six make twelve.
Therefore it is called a chapter.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 49.13 (SN 49.13, PTS SN v 245) 2.
Appamādavagga (The Chapter on Diligence)
The Chapter on Diligence (*Appamādavagga*).
[This chapter] should be expanded by way of the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*).
Its summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
The Tathāgata, the footprint,
the peak, the root, the heartwood, the jasmine,
the king, the moon, and the sun.
With "cloth" as the tenth item, they recite [the verses].
Saṃyutta Nikāya 49.23–34 (SN 49.23, PTS SN v 246), Chapter 3:
On What Is to Be Done with Strength.
The Discourse on What is to be Done with Strength, etc.:
“Bhikkhus, just as whatever tasks requiring strength are performed, they are all done depending upon the earth and established upon the earth;
even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, depending upon virtue and established upon virtue, develops the four right strivings and cultivates the four right strivings.”

And how, monks, does a monk, relying on virtue and established in virtue, develop the four right endeavors and cultivate the four right endeavors? Here, monks, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;

he exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives... [as before] ...he generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives... [as before] ...he generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives... [as before] ...he generates desire for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development of arisen wholesome states; he exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. This, monks, is how a monk, relying on virtue and established in virtue, develops the four right endeavors and cultivates the four right endeavors.

“He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk, relying on virtue and established in virtue, develops the four right strivings and cultivates the four right strivings.
(Thus the section on the factors conducive to strength should be expanded by way of the four right strivings.)
The twelfth.
The third chapter, on What is to be Done with Strength.
Its summary verse:
Strength, seed, and the nāga;
the tree, the jar, and the needle;
and with the sky, two clouds.

*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 49.35–44 (*SN* 49.35, PTS *SN* v 246). 4.
The Chapter on Searches (*Esaṇāvagga*).
The Ten Suttas on Seeking, etc.:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three seekings. What three? [The seeking of sensual pleasure, the seeking of existence, and the seeking of the holy life.]”
The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life—
these, monks, are the three searches.
For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandoning of these three searches, monks, the four right endeavors must be developed.
Which four?

Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the persistence, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;

and he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the persistence, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
“Monks, for the direct knowledge, full understanding, total destruction, and abandonment of these three searches, these four right endeavors must be developed.
[This should be expanded in detail. Tenth.
The fourth chapter: On Seeking (Esanāvagga).
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
Seeking, modes, and taints.
Existence and the three kinds of suffering;
barrenness, impurity, and distress;
feeling, craving, and thirst.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 49.45–54 (SN 49.45, PTS SN v 247) 5. Oghavagga Oghādisutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four floods. What four? The flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods. [The same formula is repeated for each of the following: bonds, ties, clingings, cravings, knots, underlying tendencies, wrong courses, stains, barbs, wastes, afflictions, fevers, arrows, attachments, and hindrances. “Bhikkhus, there are these four hindrances. What four? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor, and the hindrance of restlessness-and-worry. These, bhikkhus, are the four hindrances. “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? One who is like a mottled ox, one who is like a young ox, one who is like a bull, and one who is like a thoroughbred horse. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The detailed exposition of each follows, as in the standard suttas. “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? One who is like a mottled ox, one who is like a young ox, one who is like a bull, and one who is like a thoroughbred horse. (1) “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a mottled ox? Here, some person is reborn in a good family—one of the aristocracy, the brahmins, or the householders—and he is handsome, attractive, and graceful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion. He is well-born on both his maternal and paternal sides, of pure descent, unassailable and impeccable with respect to birth back to the seventh paternal generation. But he does not possess faith, virtue, learning, generosity, or wisdom. This is called a person like a mottled ox. (2) “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a young ox? Here, some person is reborn in a good family... of pure descent... But he possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This is called a person like a young ox. (3) “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a bull? Here, some person is reborn in a good family... of pure descent... He possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Furthermore, he is a forest-dweller, an almsfood eater, a rag-robe wearer, one who lives in the open air, one who accepts whatever seat is offered, one who eats at one sitting, one who observes the practice of eating only food in the bowl, one who observes the practice of not eating after the time, one who observes the practice of abstaining from dancing, singing, music, and shows, one who observes the practice of abstaining from wearing garlands, smartening oneself, and beautifying oneself, one who observes the practice of abstaining from high and large beds, one who observes the practice of accepting gold and silver, one who accepts gold and silver, one who engages in buying and selling, one who uses a money-lending business, one who uses the seven kinds of grain, one who uses a high bed or a large bed, one who uses a high and large bed, one who uses what is not given, one who commits sexual misconduct. This is called a person like a bull. (4) “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a thoroughbred horse? Here, some person is reborn in a good family... of pure descent... He possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Furthermore, he is a forest-dweller, an almsfood eater, a rag-robe wearer, one who lives in the open air, one who accepts whatever seat is offered, one who eats at one sitting, one who observes the practice of eating only food in the bowl, one who observes the practice of not eating after the time, one who observes the practice of abstaining from dancing, singing, music, and shows, one who observes the practice of abstaining from wearing garlands, smartening oneself, and beautifying oneself, one who observes the practice of abstaining from high and large beds, one who observes the practice of abstaining from gold and silver, one who does not accept gold and silver, one who does not engage in buying and selling, one who does not use the seven kinds of grain, one who does not use a high bed or a large bed, one who does not use a high and large bed, one who does not use what is not given, one who refrains from sexual misconduct.

This is called a person like a thoroughbred horse. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The sutta concludes with the Buddha’s praise of the person like a thoroughbred horse. *** Saṃyutta Nikāya 49.55–64 (SN 49.55, PTS SN v 248–250) 5. Oghavagga Pariññādisutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four floods. What four? The flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods. (1) “The full understanding of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the full understanding of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the full understanding of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the full understanding of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (2) “The abandoning of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the abandoning of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the abandoning of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the abandoning of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (3) “The destruction of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the destruction of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the destruction of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the destruction of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (4) “The cutting off of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the cutting off of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the cutting off of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the cutting off of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (5) “The stilling of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the stilling of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the stilling of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the stilling of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (6) “The transcendence of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the transcendence of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the transcendence of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the transcendence of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (7) “The turning away from the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the turning away from the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the turning away from the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the turning away from the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. (8) “The fading away of the flood of sensuality is the stream-entry factor of mindfulness; the fading away of the flood of existence is the stream-entry factor of investigation of phenomena; the fading away of the flood of views is the stream-entry factor of energy; the fading away of the flood of ignorance is the stream-entry factor of concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the four floods and the four factors of stream-entry. “Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters.
Which five?
Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.”
"These, monks, are the five higher fetters.
For the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandoning of these five higher fetters, monks, the four right endeavours must be developed.
Which four?"

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stabilization, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have not yet arisen; and he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
It is for the direct knowledge, full understanding, destruction, and abandonment of these five higher fetters, bhikkhus, that these four right endeavors are to be developed.”
(To be expanded in full.
Tenth. The fifth chapter, the Chapter on Floods (*Oghavagga*).
Its summary verse:
The floods, the yokes, the clingings,
the ties, and the underlying tendencies.
The strands of sensual pleasure are hindrances;
the aggregates are the lower fetters.
The fifth [section], the Connected Discourse on the Right Strivings, is concluded.
